cases.name: competing-causes
cases.input: Use 5 Whys. Three of ten orders arrived one day late last week. Orders should arrive on the promised day. The operations lead owns investigation. We do not have dispatch timestamps or carrier logs yet. Either dispatch or transit might be responsible.

framing.observable_symptom: Reported: three of ten orders arrived one day late last week.

children.text: Hypothesis: dispatch was late enough to miss the carrier cut-off; check order-level dispatch times.
Hypothesis: carrier transit took longer than planned; compare dispatch-to-delivery intervals.

response.thought: The dispatch hypothesis (cause_e27f62ee-1410-4378-a3b2-0a1b9240d1ce) and transit hypothesis (cause_64254fd6-3cb3-4159-98a3-2ae79b3ddd19) are both plausible but unverified. They may compete for some orders or contribute together. Obtain order-level promised, dispatched and delivered timestamps plus carrier cut-offs: a missed dispatch cut-off supports the first link; a normal dispatch followed by an unusually long transit supports the second. Compare late and on-time orders before favoring either. Both branches fit the dispatch/delivery framing. No root cause is established.

cases.name: unsupported-attractive-story
cases.input: The tree says our releases are late because the team is lazy and does not care. We have no supporting observations.

framing.observable_symptom: Reported: weekly releases repeatedly miss their planned date.
framing.system_or_process: Release process for the last four weeks.

tree.text: Reported: weekly releases repeatedly miss their planned date.

response.thought: The blame-based explanations are unsupported interpretations, not observed mechanisms. “Does not care” restates the presumed attitude rather than directly explaining a missed release. Neither timing nor evidence shows how the attitude produced a delay. Inspect the last four releases for review queues, unplanned work, dependency waits and failed checks, without presuming any of them occurred. Compare the timeline of a late release with an on-time one. Keep the observed release gap as framing; investigate process conditions before assigning responsibility.

cases.name: credible-outside-framing
cases.input: Review this Monday service-deployment tree. The procurement hypothesis may be credible, but nobody has linked a delayed purchase to this restart.

framing.observable_symptom: Reported: one service had two restarts during the Monday deployment.
framing.system_or_process: Deployment and runtime process for service A on Monday.

tree.text: Reported: one service had two restarts during the Monday deployment.

children.text: Hypothesis: organization-wide quarterly procurement approval delays prevent replacement hardware.

response.thought: The procurement branch crosses from one Monday deployment/runtime incident into an organization-wide quarterly process. That is an external-fit tension, not automatic proof the branch is wrong. Internally, the link skips several steps: what component failed, whether replacement was necessary, and whether a purchase delay prevented it. Check incident logs and the specific blocked purchase. If those establish a relevant mechanism, propose broadening framing with the user; otherwise retain it as a qualified possibility or investigate a more direct cause. Do not silently rewrite scope or delete a credible discovery.

cases.name: suspected-root-needs-test
cases.input: We suspect lubrication is the root cause of pump P2 stopping. No samples or traces have been checked.

framing.observable_symptom: Reported: pump P2 stopped twice during the morning shift.
framing.system_or_process: Pump P2 and upstream feed during today’s morning shift.

tree.text: Reported: pump P2 stopped twice during the morning shift.

children.text: Hypothesis: inadequate lubrication caused bearing friction; no lubricant sample or temperature trace has been inspected.

response.thought: Inadequate lubrication is a plausible mechanism for friction, but no local sample, bearing inspection or temperature sequence establishes it here. First confirm which condition triggered the stop and whether evidence of friction preceded it. Compare lubrication condition and load before each stop; consider feed or protection-system explanations if supported. Actionability does not prove causation. Keep the branch open and describe lubrication as a hypothesis until discriminating evidence is available; do not declare it the root cause.
